title: Work on your character (Akhlaq)
whyMatters: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said, 'I was sent to perfect good character.' Rituals are part of Islam, and so is how you treat people, how you carry yourself, and who you turn into. Good character (akhlaq) is what real faith grows into. When your prayers and your fasting start changing how you deal with the world, when you catch yourself being more patient or more honest than you used to be, that is Islam showing up in an ordinary day. The Prophet also taught that 'the best among you are those who have the best character,' and 'actions are judged by intentions.' What happens inside you counts as much as what anybody can see.

subSteps: Sabr (patience): holding steady through difficulty. Life will test you, and this is the tool you reach for most.
Sidq (truthfulness): honesty in what you say and what you do, including when it costs you something.
Tawadu (humility): knowing every good thing came from Allah, and treating people well whatever their status.
Ihsan (excellence): doing things carefully and sincerely, as though Allah is watching, because He is.
Shukr (gratitude): noticing what you have and thanking Allah and the people around you for it.
Rahmah (mercy and compassion): kindness towards everything Allah made, animals and the land included.

exactActions.text: Study the Prophet as your example
subSteps: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is described in the Quran as 'an excellent example' (33:21).
Read about his character: how gentle he was with children, how fair in business, how kind to his neighbors, how patient with the people who opposed him.
Start with a short biography (seerah). 'Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources' by Martin Lings is the one people usually hand you first.
Pay attention to how he handled conflict, treated the poor, and forgave the people who wronged him.
Pick one part of his character each week and work on that in your own life.

exactActions.text: Put it into practice every day
subSteps: Start the day with an intention (niyyah) to hold to one virtue, maybe patience or gratitude.
When you feel anger rising, remember the hadith: 'The strong person is not the one who can wrestle, but the one who controls themselves at the time of anger.'
Do small kind things. Smile at a stranger, help a neighbor, actually listen when someone is talking to you.
Before you act or speak, pause and ask yourself: would the Prophet (peace be upon him) approve of this?
At night, look back over the day. Where did it go well? Where could it have gone better? This self-reflection (muhasabah) was a practice of the companions of the Prophet.
Islam puts enormous weight on keeping family ties (silat al-rahm), including with family who are not Muslim.
Be at your best with family, neighbors, coworkers, and strangers alike.
The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The best of you are those who are best to their families.'
If someone wrongs you, try to answer with patience instead of getting even. Forgiveness sits near the top of the virtues.
Your character is often the most effective da'wah (invitation to Islam) you will ever do, because people watch how you live.

exactActions.text: Be kind to yourself about old habits
subSteps: Everybody brings habits from before Islam that do not fit where they are now.
Change does not happen overnight. Take one habit at a time.
Swap a bad habit for a better one. Gossip, for instance, can become dhikr (remembrance of Allah).
If you slip, make istighfar (ask Allah for forgiveness) and try again. Allah loves those who repent.
Keep company with people whose character you want, because you end up like the people you spend time with.

timeEstimate: A lifetime. Daily practice, and it keeps going

obstacles.problem: I keep falling back into old habits
obstacles.solution: This is part of being human rather than a sign of failure. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that all human beings make mistakes, and that the best of them are the ones who repent. Every time you catch a slip and try again, you have grown. Aim at progress instead of perfection. Some habits took years to build and will take a while to unpick, so be gentle with yourself while you do it.

Patience (sabr) is one of the most mentioned virtues in the Quran, partly because it is one of the hardest. It strengthens with use, like a muscle. When impatience rises, take a breath and say 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' (Indeed, to Allah we belong and to Him we return). Start with the small tests, traffic and long queues and minor annoyances, then work up from there.

obstacles.problem: I find non-Muslim social settings hard now
obstacles.solution: You do not have to withdraw from non-Muslim friends or social circles. Islam encourages good relationships with everyone. Set the boundaries you need, like politely turning down a drink, without preaching at anybody. Your character in those rooms is worship in itself. Most people respect someone who is straightforward about who they are, so be yourself and let your faith steer it.

obstacles.problem: I don't feel like I'm changing fast enough
obstacles.solution: Spiritual growth is rarely dramatic. It is slow and hard to see from the inside, even while other people notice it. Keep a simple journal and read it back once a month, and you will find progress that was invisible day to day. The companions of the Prophet took years to build their character, and they had the best teacher in history. Trust the process and trust Allah's timing for you.

obstacles.problem: I feel like a hypocrite because my actions don't match my beliefs
obstacles.solution: Feeling that tension is a sign of healthy faith. A real hypocrite does not care about the gap between what they believe and what they do. The fact that it bothers you means your conscience is awake and working. Close the gap one step at a time, and make du'a for sincerity (ikhlas). Allah is looking at your heart and your effort rather than the tally.

tinyVersion: Take one virtue for the week. Be more patient, or more honest, or more grateful. Character is Islam in motion.
unlocksNext: As your character grows, so does the appetite to learn more. The next step is about making a lifelong habit of seeking knowledge and understanding Islam better.
